edges.description: The substitution alters the channel so that it conducts cations.
The same substitution impairs the protein's native ammonia-transport function.
The open pore admits a transmembrane leak of monovalent cations.
The leak admits sodium and loses potassium across the membrane.
Stomatin is lost from the mature OHSt red cell membrane as a secondary effect of the disorder, not as its cause.
The cell upregulates active cation pumping to counter the gain.
Net cation gain draws water osmotically into the cell.
Sustained pumping consumes ATP and drives glycolysis to exhaustion.
The overhydrated cell adopts the cup-shaped stomatocyte form.
Swelling raises the mean corpuscular volume.
Added water dilutes intracellular haemoglobin.
The shape change is seen on the blood film as stomatocytosis.
The reduced surface-to-volume ratio stiffens the cell.
The overhydrated cell lyses at near-physiological tonicity.
Poorly deformable cells are trapped in the splenic microcirculation.
Sequestered cells are destroyed outside the circulation.
Red cell loss outstripping production causes the anaemia.
The marrow responds to haemolysis with reticulocytosis.
Haem catabolism from destroyed cells raises unconjugated bilirubin.
Sustained erythrophagocytosis enlarges the spleen.
Chronic haemolysis contributes to the tendency to iron overload.
Accumulated iron raises hepatic iron concentration.
Thromboembolic disease, particularly after splenectomy, drives chronic pulmonary hypertension.
The prothrombotic state predisposes to thromboembolic events, especially after splenectomy.
Raised bilirubin produces clinical jaundice.
Reproduces the gain-of-function cation conductance of the mutant pore.

nodes.description: The Na,K-ATPase runs at greatly increased activity in an attempt to restore normal cation gradients against the leak, pumping far more than normal red cells. The compensation is insufficient to prevent the net gain and swelling.

evidence.reference_title: The Molecular Basis for Altered Cation Permeability in Hereditary Stomatocytic Human Red Blood Cells.
evidence.snippet: This is consistent with an increased energy demand in OHSt cells, possibly resulting from elevated activity of the Na,K-ATPase attempting to maintain normal cation gradients.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary stomatocytes contain 2-10-fold more cation pumps than normal and the increased active cation pumping may explain the high ADP, the low 2,3-diphosphoglycerate concentration and the increased oxygen affinity in this syndrome.

nodes.description: The ATP demand of continual compensatory pumping overworks the only ATP source the red cell has, glycolysis. A metabolomic study of OHSt patients found glycolysis exhausted, with accumulation of ADP, pyruvate, lactate and malate, leaving the cell metabolically vulnerable. A branch consequence of the compensation.

nodes.description: Through the mutant pore the red cell membrane leaks monovalent cations. In OHSt this is the most severe leak of the hereditary stomatocytoses, up to about 40 times the normal basal rate at body temperature, and it increases linearly with temperature, consistent with a constitutively open cation channel.

nodes.description: Water follows the net cation gain into the cell osmotically, so the erythrocyte becomes overhydrated and swollen. The overhydration is the direct cause of the raised cell volume and lowered intracellular haemoglobin concentration that are the laboratory signature of the disease.

This is a loss-of-function for the protein's physiological substrate and is a branch consequence rather than part of the haemolytic chain.

nodes.description: OHSt red cells are near-completely deficient in the 32 kDa membrane protein stomatin (band 7.2b), the finding after which the protein was originally named. No mutation in the stomatin gene is found; the protein is mis-trafficked and lost on erythroid maturation. This is a secondary correlate of the primary RhAG defect, a dead-end branch that does not drive the haemolysis.
